idea/want: Say you want a network that draws new handwritten digits, not copies of the ones it has seen.
idea/z: Give it a list of random numbers, z, and let it turn them into a picture. Each new z gives a new picture.
idea/stuck: But training needs a loss, and a new digit has no right answer to compare with: there is no formula for how real a picture looks.
idea/judge: In 2014, Ian Goodfellow and colleagues found a way: train a second network to be the judge.
idea/police: Their paper compares it to counterfeiters printing fake money and police learning to spot it: the contest drives both to improve, until the fakes pass for real.
idea/G: The network that draws is the generator, G: it generates the pictures.
idea/D: The judge is the discriminator, D, from discriminate: to tell apart. It gives the probability that a picture is real.
idea/name: Two networks as adversaries, opponents in a contest: a generative adversarial network, or GAN.
dstep/binary: D sorts pictures into two classes, real and fake: a binary classifier, binary meaning of two.
dstep/one: So one number is enough: a sigmoid at the end gives the probability of real, between zero and one, and fake gets the rest, one minus it.
dstep/labels: Each picture's right answer, called its label, is one for real and zero for fake.
dstep/real: Say D gives a real image zero point eight. Its cross-entropy is minus the log of the probability on the right answer: minus the log of zero point eight, about zero point two two.
dstep/fake: And it gives a fake zero point three. A fake's right answer is fake, whose probability is one minus zero point three: zero point seven.
dstep/fakeloss: So its loss is minus the log of zero point seven: about zero point three six.
dstep/sum: D's loss is the two together: zero point five eight. Its gradient step pushes the real score up and the fake score down, while G's weights stay fixed.
gstep/flip: Then it is G's turn. G is trained as if its fake were labeled real: its loss is minus the log of D of G of z, D's score on the fake G makes from z.
gstep/gnum: At zero point three, that is about one point two zero: the lower D's score on the fake, the bigger G's loss.
gstep/whynot: Why not just have G push D's loss up? The 2014 paper explains: early on, D rejects the poor fakes with confidence, far out on its sigmoid's flat end.
gstep/flat: There, D's loss on a fake is flat, so G would get almost no gradient. Minus the log of D keeps a steady slope, so G learns from the start.
gstep/back: The gradient flows back through D, held fixed, into G. Only G's weights change, so D's scores on real images, which never pass through G, stay put.
gstep/alternate: The steps alternate, one for D, then one for G, so neither gets far ahead of the other.
collapse/modes: Real digits come in ten kinds: plot how often each kind turns up, and there are ten peaks. In statistics, the most common value is the mode, so ten peaks make ten modes.
collapse/one: Now say G finds one fake that fools D: a convincing seven. Its loss asks only that each fake fool D, not for variety, so it draws that seven for every z.
collapse/name: Each picture looks real, but the variety is gone: the output has collapsed onto one mode. That is mode collapse.
collapse/warned: The 2014 paper already warns of it: train G too much without updating D, and G collapses too many values of z onto the same picture.
